To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the equine gastrointestinal tract contains distinct luminal microbial communities that are regionally distributed throughout the length of this organ and (2) mucosal microbial communities are more similar throughout the length of a healthy equine gut than those of the lumen.

the luminal microbiota of the equine small intestine and stomach are distinct from those of the large intestine and that the mucosal microbiota of the small and large intestine are more similar to each other than to the lumenal microbiota.
the equine gut microbiota is composed of a highly diverse community of bacteria, and that this diversity is highest in the small intestine and colon, and is lower in the stomach and large intestine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a microbiological map of the healthy equide gastrointestinal tract.
the microbiome in horses.
the microbiota of the equine gastrointestinal tract and how it relates to disease states.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the microbiota present within luminal contents of each of the regions of the equine gastrointestinal tract are highly variable, while the mucosal microbial communities are more similar throughout the gut.
the microbiota of the equine small intestine is distinct from the microbiota of both the equine large intestine and feces.
the equine microbiome is a dynamic entity that is influenced by the location within the gastrointestinal tract, as well as the luminal or mucosal compartment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the equine microbiome is a complex ecosystem with a high degree of regional variation.

the luminal microbiota is highly variable throughout the equine gastrointestinal tract and that this is especially true in the stomach, small intestine and cecum, whereas the mucosal microbiota is relatively uniform throughout the equine large bowel.
the luminal and the mucosal microbial populations are different, and that luminal populations are more variable than mucosal ones.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fecal samples do not accurately represent the microbiota present within any of the regions of the equine gastrointestinal tract.
the microbiota of the equine gastrointestinal tract is highly heterogeneous and that a single sampling site may not be representative of the entire gastrointestinal tract.
the microbiota in the equine gut is highly diverse and variable, and this variability is not uniform throughout the gastrointestinal tract.
